title: Output-file aggregate bound counts only data bytes: many zero-byte files bypass it and collection runs unbounded past the code timeout
description: The a80b830 fix added MAX_TOTAL_OUTPUT_FILE_BYTES (200 MB) to _collect_output_files, but it accumulates only file data lengths (total += len(data)). Sandboxed code, chosen by any client that can reach the unauthenticated run_python_code tool or by a prompt-injected LLM, can fill ./output with a very large number of zero- or tiny-byte files. Each is opened, fstat'ed, read, type-guessed, and turned into a content item (File/Image/Audio) by the shared server process, yet adds 0 to the budget. There is no cap on entry count and no cap on serialized (JSON) size. Collection also runs after proc.wait() with no deadline of its own, so the server keeps doing this work well after the code timeout has elapsed. Independently reproduced in the real srt+bwrap Docker-mode setup: an 8 s code-timeout run created 9,598 zero-byte files; _collect_output_files then ran 9.82 s after the timeout (tool call wall 21.4 s vs 8 s advertised timeout), returned 9,598 items and 3,176,938 JSON bytes, grew server RSS by 14.4 MB, and charged 0 bytes to the 200 MB budget. A faster filesystem (h-output evidence1) yielded 40,940 files, 21.14 s post-timeout collection, 13,551,140 JSON bytes, +55.7 MB RSS. Cost scales with file-creation speed within code_timeout_seconds and multiplies across concurrent requests, all in the one shared server process.
root_cause: code_executor.py:201-204 enforce the aggregate limit only on len(data), so zero-byte entries always pass and never consume budget; line 188 enumerates every entry of the sandbox-writable output dir with no entry-count limit; and line 254 calls _collect_output_files after proc.wait() (line 160) with no time bound. Entry count, filename length, and per-item object/JSON overhead are never charged against any bound.
intended_behavior: Returned output should be bounded in aggregate by entry count and total serialized size (including names and encoding overhead), not just raw data bytes, and server-side collection should stop at a fixed budget and not run unbounded after the code timeout, so one run cannot make the shared server do unbounded work or hold memory past its timeout.

Every entry name in output/ is listed and iterated; there is no entry-count limit.
The budget check only compares data length; a zero-byte file adds 0 to total and always passes.
A content object is appended per entry (File here, Image/Audio at 210/214) and later serialized into the MCP response by the shared server process.

evidence.description: MAX_TOTAL_OUTPUT_FILE_BYTES is the only aggregate limit; there is no count or serialized-size constant.
total += len(data): empty files never consume budget.
The code timeout covers only proc.wait; collection at line 254 happens afterwards with no time bound (observed 9.82 s local / 21.14 s h-output, post-timeout).
ulimit -f bounds single-file size only; inode or entry count is not limited.

How many entries can be created depends on the run-dir filesystem's file-creation speed within code_timeout_seconds (default 30 s); post-timeout collection time and returned item count scale linearly and add up across concurrent requests.

Wrap _collect_output_files to measure its wall time, the number of returned items, the summed model_dump_json length, and /proc/self/statm RSS growth; also record the total tool-call wall time vs the code timeout.

Server takedown was not attempted; the residual is a shared worker held well past the timeout plus tens of MB per request, scaling with fs speed and concurrency.

Also check st_size from fstat before reading so files that would go over budget are not read at all.

title: Sandboxed code and MCP callers can inject raw terminal escape sequences into the operator's server log stream
description: _collect_output_files logs the name of every ./output entry it skips as the structlog field name=. It skips symlinks and other entries that cannot be opened with O_NOFOLLOW (code_executor.py:192), non-regular or hard-linked entries (197), and oversized files (202). run_python_code also logs the caller-supplied code string as code= (240). The shared logger (utils/logger.py:24) uses structlog.dev.ConsoleRenderer with the default repr_native_str=False, and PrintLoggerFactory (line 28) writes to the server's stdout. In the installed structlog 26.1.0 (dev.py:915-928), ConsoleRenderer._repr repr-quotes a str value only if it contains a space, tab, '=', CR, LF or a quote character. A value made of ESC/BEL-based sequences is therefore written to stdout byte for byte. Examples are ESC c (full terminal reset), CSI cursor-up plus erase-line, and OSC 0 (set window title). The README shows the server run in the foreground (`docker run -p 6400:6400 ...`, or the `mcp-run-isolated-python` CLI), so this stdout is normally the operator's terminal or `docker logs`. Untrusted sandboxed code, or an unauthenticated MCP client through code=, can therefore reset the operator's terminal, erase or overwrite earlier log lines, and change the window title. OSC 52 clipboard writes are possible where the terminal allows them, but they were not tested. The conflicting h-misc (u6) negative result is explained by its test values: they contained spaces and newlines, which force repr quoting.
root_cause: The shared renderer prints untrusted str field values without escaping them. structlog.dev.ConsoleRenderer is built without repr_native_str=True (utils/logger.py:24), and code_executor.py passes names chosen by the sandbox (lines 192, 197, 202) and the tool argument (line 240) as native str fields. structlog escapes only whitespace, '=' and quote characters, not other control bytes.
intended_behavior: Values from the sandbox or the tool call should appear in operator logs only in escaped form, so they can never act as terminal control sequences.

title: TOCTOU in _remove_run_dir: a surviving sandbox descendant can make the unsandboxed server chmod any same-uid file or directory outside the run dir to 0700 (macOS CLI/library mode)
description: _remove_run_dir (code_executor.py:59-71) runs in the trusted server process, outside the srt sandbox, from the finally block of run_python_code. It does a top-down os.walk over the run directory. For each name in `dirs` it checks `is_symlink()` (an lstat, line 66) and then calls path-based `Path.chmod(stat.S_IRWXU)` (line 68). Path.chmod follows symlinks. The run directory is the sandbox's writable cwd (Popen cwd=code_path at line 141; allowWrite ['.'] in default_srt_settings.json line 10). So a sandbox process that is still alive during cleanup can swap a real subdirectory entry for a symlink between the check and the chmod, and the server then applies mode 0700 to the symlink's target outside the run dir. The target can be a directory or a regular file: os.walk classifies the entry when it scans the directory, and the swap happens after that, so the chmod lands on whatever the link points to. The sandbox cannot chmod outside its write scope itself, so this is a confused-deputy escape from the sandbox's write confinement, limited to setting mode exactly 0700 on objects the server uid owns. Verifier results: (1) Running the real, unmodified _remove_run_dir against a concurrent racer process in the parent sandbox, with 1 CPU, the race was won almost at once. A dummy directory outside the run dir went 0o555 -> 0o700 after 28 cleanup iterations (agents/ver-macrace/artifacts/evidence1.txt). A dummy regular file went 0o444 -> 0o700 after 9 iterations (agents/ver-macrace/artifacts/evidence3.txt). The hunter's third decisive fact (the window is winnable) is therefore settled locally, and the hunter's claim of 'directories only' is wrong. (2) In the Linux/Docker deployment (real srt+bwrap, user=nonroot, server root), a double-forked, setsid'd descendant did not survive a normal run exit (none alive afterwards; agents/ver-macrace/artifacts/evidence2.txt). The Linux/Docker path therefore has no racer, and the issue is limited to macOS (Seatbelt, no pid namespace, user=None). The root cause is distinct from u14. Descendant survival is only the prerequisite, and a setsid'd descendant leaves the process group, so even an os.killpg(proc.pid) on normal exit would not remove it. The sink here is the check-then-path-chmod pair. This fingerprint overlaps with the rmtree fingerprint only in that both fixes touch the same walk. The fix here specifically needs a no-follow, fd-relative chmod.
claimed_root_cause: code_executor.py:66-68 checks is_symlink() (lstat by path) and then calls Path.chmod(stat.S_IRWXU) by path, which follows symlinks (os.chmod with follow_symlinks=True). The two are separate path-resolving syscalls on a sandbox-writable directory tree, and nothing does an O_NOFOLLOW/dir_fd-relative open or an fstat identity check between them. A sandbox descendant that is still running during cleanup can put a symlink into the window, and the unsandboxed server's chmod then goes to an arbitrary same-uid path.

Path.chmod(stat.S_IRWXU) is called without follow_symlinks=False and resolves by path. The unshare wrapper applies only when sys.platform == 'linux'. On macOS there is no pid-namespace containment of descendants.

This was refuted for Linux/Docker (evidence2) but is unverified on macOS.

title: On macOS (Seatbelt backend), processes started by sandboxed code outlive the run: nothing kills them on normal exit, a setsid() child escapes the timeout killpg, and survivors that keep stdio pin reader threads and pipe fds in the server
description: At a80b830, CodeExecutor._run_sandboxed starts srt with start_new_session=True. It sends os.killpg(proc.pid, SIGKILL) only in the TimeoutExpired branch (code_executor.py:161-166), and the comment there relies on bwrap --die-with-parent. The interpreter command gets the unshare prefix only when sys.platform == 'linux' (code_executor.py:245-249). That prefix creates IPC and user namespaces, not a PID namespace. So on darwin the only containment for descendants is membership in the process group. From source, on the macOS backend (srt 0.0.64 sandbox-exec with process-fork and process-exec allowed, no PID namespace, and srt's cli.js calls process.exit when its direct child exits, with no tree kill): (a) when a run exits normally, a background child is never signalled, proc.wait returns, the run dir is removed and the tool returns; (b) on timeout, a descendant that called setsid()/setpgid() is outside the killed group. The survivor keeps running under the Seatbelt profile, as the server uid (in host CLI mode user defaults to None, so that is the invoking user), with no deadline. If it keeps the inherited stdout/stderr write ends, _drain blocks in read(65536) forever. reader.join(timeout=5) then gives up, the call is delayed about 10 s, buffered stdout is dropped, and 2 daemon threads and 2 pipe fds stay in the server for each such run. This is a possible path to fd exhaustion when the server's RLIMIT_NOFILE is low (macOS commonly defaults the soft limit to 256; not verified for deployments). Each detached process needs one request from any MCP client that can reach the server, or from a prompt-injected LLM. The per-run 'ulimit -u 256' added in a80b830 is not a lifecycle control. RLIMIT_NPROC is checked against the uid's total process count at fork time. It blocks the fork only when the server uid already has 256 or more processes (the dev host uid has 433) and never applies to uid 0. A dedicated service account with fewer processes can still fork. The executor-side lifecycle was reproduced with a stub srt that has no Seatbelt (agents/h-macos/artifacts/evidence1.txt): normal exit left a survivor, 10.3 s delay, output '', threads 1->3, fds 4->6; a timeout with a setsid child left a survivor; the control with no setsid was killed. Linux and Docker are not affected: at current source with real srt+bwrap (user=nonroot), neither the normal-exit+setsid child nor the timeout+setsid child survived, and threads and fds returned to baseline (agents/ver-macdetach/artifacts/evidence1.txt).
claimed_root_cause: code_executor._run_sandboxed contains the sandbox's process tree only with a process-group SIGKILL on the timeout path. For everything else it relies on bwrap's PID namespace and --die-with-parent, which exist only on Linux. On normal exit there is no group or session kill, nothing tracks descendants that leave the group, and the drain pipes are never closed after reader.join times out. srt's macOS backend (sandbox-exec) provides neither a PID namespace nor a tree kill, and the a80b830 'ulimit -u' is a per-uid fork quota, not a lifetime bound.

trace.description: Caller-supplied Python code is passed to CodeExecutor.run_python_code. The unauthenticated MCP tool run_python_code (mcp_server.py) reaches the same executor.
The unshare prefix is added only when sys.platform == 'linux', and it adds no PID namespace anyway. On darwin cmd is 'ulimit -u 256 ...; ulimit -f ...; exec "<python>" "<code.py>"'.
start_new_session=True puts srt in a new session and process group. This is the only descendant containment the executor adds.
proc.wait returns when srt exits, and srt exits when its direct child exits. Nothing is killed on the normal-exit path.
On timeout only, os.killpg(proc.pid, SIGKILL) reaches members of the original group. It misses a descendant that has called setsid()/setpgid().
reader.join(timeout=5) gives up while a survivor holds the inherited pipe write ends. The daemon threads and the proc.stdout/proc.stderr fds are never closed.
The run dir is removed and the call returns while the detached sandboxed processes keep running as the server uid with no deadline.

evidence.description: killpg exists only in the TimeoutExpired handler (161-166). The normal-exit path does no group or session cleanup.
The comment shows the design relies on bwrap --die-with-parent, which is Linux only.
_drain blocks in stream.read(65536) until EOF, which never arrives while a descendant holds the pipe.
'ulimit -u 256' is RLIMIT_NPROC. It is counted per uid, only fails a fork when the uid already has 256 or more processes (not enforced for uid 0), and does not bound process lifetime.
test_timeout_kills_all_sandboxed_processes (49-64) covers only a same-pgid child on the timeout path, not setsid() or normal exit.
Claims 'own pid namespace', which holds only for the Linux bwrap backend.
user defaults to None (passed through at 143), so in host CLI mode survivors run as the invoking user.

blockers: Real macOS Seatbelt behaviour was not observed. sandbox-exec cannot run in the approved Linux container sandbox, and target or srt code must not run on the macOS host. From source, srt 0.0.64 macos-sandbox-utils.js:284-287 allows process-fork and process-exec, and cli.js:202-230 spawns with stdio 'inherit' and exits on direct-child exit with no descendant cleanup. However, survival past srt exit and killpg was shown only with a stub srt that has no Seatbelt (agents/h-macos/artifacts/evidence1.txt). The Linux control at current source left no survivors (agents/ver-macdetach/artifacts/evidence1.txt).

title: Every run leaves srt temp dirs and sockets in shared /tmp because TMPDIR is not set (CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR does not cover them)
description: _run_sandboxed starts srt with env={PATH, CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR=<run dir>}. On Linux, srt 0.0.64 creates its per-run bubblewrap mask dirs (claude-empty-*) and its proxy sockets (claude-http-*.sock, srt-mux-*.sock) under node's os.tmpdir(). That reads TMPDIR, and without it falls back to /tmp. Nothing removes these entries, neither on normal exit nor after the SIGKILL on timeout. _remove_run_dir only cleans the run dir. Each tool call therefore leaves about 3-4 entries in the server's /tmp for good: roughly 2 empty 0700 dirs plus 1-2 stale sockets. Any MCP caller can cause this with a trivial payload. The effect is slow inode and directory-block growth in the shared /tmp (the container's writable layer in Docker mode, the host /tmp in CLI mode). Recovery needs manual cleanup or recreating the container or host tmp. Sandboxed code cannot write /tmp itself, so this retained growth is caused by the server. Sandboxed code can list /tmp and see the names of these leftovers, but they are empty dirs or stale sockets with no content. This is a low-severity resource-retention issue, not a data exposure.

title: Per-run process caps are not sized against the shared container pid pool and there is no limit on concurrent runs, so two unauthenticated requests make other clients' runs fail (and runs still have no memory bound)
description: Commit a80b830 added `ulimit -u 256` and `ulimit -f` in front of each sandboxed interpreter. The hunter said RLIMIT_NPROC is one pool per uid shared by all runs. That is refuted on Linux. The ulimit is applied just before `unshare --user` gives each run a new user namespace, and kernel ucounts (5.14 and later) then charge the limit per run. Verified under real srt+bwrap on kernel 6.8: an attacker run stopped at its own cap while a concurrent run of the same uid 999 still forked 10 children (agents/ver-limits/artifacts/evidence1.txt). The hunter's reproduction never reached the 256 cap. Its attacker stopped at 102 processes because it exhausted the fixture's 128-pid container cgroup. The underlying root cause is still present, though. Each run's cap is not sized against the shared container pid pool, and nothing limits how many runs execute at once. run_python_code runs in the framework thread pool with no semaphore or per-caller cap. Under the shipped compose file (pids_limit 512, 256 per run), two concurrent unauthenticated runs are enough to use up the pool. In any deployment whose container pid limit is at or below 256, one run is enough. After that, the server's own subprocess.Popen for another client's run fails with EAGAIN. The broad except turns this into 'Tool run failed. Do not call this tool again, inform the user that it is broken.' This was reproduced at scaled values: a per-run cap of 60 against a 128-pid pool, with two attacker runs and a concurrent victim run (agents/ver-limits/artifacts/evidence2.txt). The server process stays up. Service recovers once the attacker runs end (at most code_timeout_seconds, 30s by default), and resubmitting sustains the outage. The code comment says the cap exists to keep a fork bomb from starving the server. The server's ability to start runs is exactly what gets starved, so the owner's stated intent is not met. Runs also still have no memory bound (no ulimit -v, RLIMIT_AS or per-run cgroup). That part is source-visible only and was not reproduced here. It is contained only where a container memory limit exists. The README `docker run` command sets none, and there it can reach host memory. On macOS CLI mode the unshare wrapper is absent, so `ulimit -u` there counts against the host user's per-uid total. That was not verified.
root_cause: The only per-run limits are the shell ulimits in run_python_code (code_executor.py:242-243, MAX_SANDBOX_PROCESSES=256 at :36). _run_sandboxed (code_executor.py:139-150) starts each run with Popen and has no memory limit or per-run cgroup. run_python_code has no admission control: no semaphore, no concurrency cap, no per-caller limit. The per-run caps therefore add up with no bound against the one container pid pool (docker-compose.yml pids_limit 512; none in the README `docker run`). The server's own fork for new runs draws from that same pool, and memory has no per-run bound at all.
intended_behavior: A run that hits its quota should fail only itself. The server must always keep headroom to start runs for other clients. Concretely: (per-run cap × maximum concurrent runs) + server overhead must stay below the container pid and memory limits, or each run must get its own cgroup (pids.max/memory.max). Extra runs beyond that are rejected or queued.

title: No concurrent-run admission control: 40 concurrent long runs from one unauthenticated client fill FastMCP's shared 40-thread pool and delay every other client's tool calls
description: run_python_code is a synchronous tool (code_executor.py:224-225). FastMCP 4.0.3 runs it through call_sync_fn_in_threadpool (fastmcp/tools/function_tool.py:477), which calls anyio.to_thread.run_sync without a limiter (fastmcp/utilities/async_utils.py:34). That means it uses anyio's default process-wide CapacityLimiter(40) (anyio/_backends/_asyncio.py:3038), and nothing in the repo overrides it. Each call keeps its worker thread for the whole run, because proc.wait(timeout=code_timeout_seconds) at code_executor.py:160 blocks, 30 s by default. The repo has no semaphore, per-caller cap, or busy rejection anywhere (mcp_server.py:26-56). A local test used the real run_mcp HTTP server, the real FastMCP dispatch and the real run_python_code. Only the sandbox subprocess was replaced by an 8 s sleep, standing in for the proc.wait hold. With 39 attacker calls in flight, a victim call took 8.02 s, which is just its own run. With 40 attacker calls in flight, it took 14.62 s: it waited about 6.6 s in the queue for an attacker's slot to free up. So any client that can reach the unauthenticated endpoint can delay all other clients by up to code_timeout_seconds per wave with 40 cheap sleeping runs. Sending new waves keeps the delay going for as long as the attacker keeps sending. It recovers on its own once the attacker stops. The shipped per-run `ulimit -u 256` does not stop this. A sleeping run forks nothing after the ulimit (`exec` at code_executor.py:250), and srt/bwrap are started from the server process, outside the limit. This is separate from no-per-run-resource-limits. That finding is about per-uid process accounting and makes victim runs fail. This one is about queueing for the shared worker pool, and it needs no process exhaustion. In docker-compose deployments, pids_limit 512 kicks in first (a real srt run uses about 21 tasks, so about 24 concurrent runs), and later runs fail rather than queue. The 40-thread starvation is therefore the binding limit for CLI deployments and for the README `docker run` command, which sets no pids limit.
root_cause: The only limit on concurrent code runs is the framework's implicit default: anyio's process-wide 40-token thread limiter, shared with every other sync tool call. The application never adds its own admission control, per-caller or per-client concurrency quota, or fast busy rejection. Each admitted run keeps its slot for up to code_timeout_seconds (code_executor.py:160, 224; mcp_server.py:26-42, 49-56).
intended_behavior: One lower-trust caller should not be able to take every execution slot on a shared multi-user server. Concurrent runs should be limited per principal or per client, with a clear busy response, and there should be spare capacity so other clients' calls are not silently queued behind one caller's long-running jobs.

title: Sandboxed code can make its run directory survive cleanup by creating a very deep directory tree (the a80b830 unlock-then-rmtree fix is incomplete)
description: _remove_run_dir unlocks directories with a path-based os.walk and a Path.is_symlink()/Path.chmod pair, then calls shutil.rmtree(ignore_errors=True). The sandboxed code decides how deep the tree in its run dir goes. It can build it with dir_fd-relative mkdir, so no path limit applies while it writes. Once a subdirectory path is longer than PATH_MAX, Path.is_symlink() raises OSError ENAMETOOLONG. Python 3.13 pathlib re-raises that errno, and the call sits outside the contextlib.suppress block. The exception escapes _remove_run_dir and the finally block of run_python_code before shutil.rmtree runs, so the whole run dir and everything in it stays on disk. Trees shorter than PATH_MAX but deeper than the free fd budget are also left behind: Python 3.13 rmtree holds one fd per level, and ignore_errors hides the EMFILE. That case only logs 'Could not fully remove run directory', and the tool still reports success. Every call can leave data behind permanently, and repeated calls fill the server's working-directory filesystem. This applies in the shipped Docker mode (server root, code nonroot) and also in same-uid mode.
root_cause: The cleanup code assumes a tree shape that is safe for path-based walking and for recursion that holds one fd per level, but the sandbox controls that shape completely. code_executor.py:66 calls (Path(root) / name).is_symlink() without catching OSError, so ENAMETOOLONG propagates out of _remove_run_dir before shutil.rmtree at line 69 runs. shutil.rmtree(ignore_errors=True) at line 69 silently gives up on EMFILE. There is no fallback removal and no guard around the cleanup as a whole. Lines 70-71 only log.
intended_behavior: The run directory and everything the sandbox wrote are always removed at the end of each run, whatever tree shape, depth or permission bits the sandbox created. A cleanup error must never skip the removal or replace the tool result.

trace.description: code_executor.run_python_code is registered as the MCP tool, so python_code comes from any MCP caller (the HTTP transport has no auth). direct_use.py reaches the same method.
The caller's code runs under srt with write access to its run dir. There it builds a directory tree 2100 levels deep with dir_fd-relative mkdir, which is never limited by PATH_MAX.
_remove_run_dir(code_path) is called unguarded in the finally block

os.walk yields a root path longer than PATH_MAX. Path.is_symlink() -> lstat raises OSError ENAMETOOLONG (Python 3.13 pathlib does not ignore that errno), outside contextlib.suppress. The exception leaves the function and the finally block.
shutil.rmtree is never reached in the deeper-than-PATH_MAX case. In the shorter-than-PATH_MAX case it fails on EMFILE, and ignore_errors hides that. Either way the run dir and its files stay on disk.

is_symlink() is outside the contextlib.suppress(OSError) block, which only wraps chmod at lines 67-68

If the path still exists afterwards, fall back to depth-safe fts-based tools that are available on both GNU and BSD/macOS: `chmod -R -P -- u+rwx <path>` (unlocks each directory at its preorder visit before it is entered, does not follow symlinks), then `rm -rf -- <path>`. Neither holds one fd per level or builds paths longer than PATH_MAX. Put `--` before the mode operand: BSD getopt stops at the first non-option, so a `--` placed after the mode becomes a stray file operand relative to the server's cwd. Do not switch the unlock to os.open()+fchmod: opening a mode-0 directory fails without DAC_OVERRIDE, which breaks the same-uid unlock that a80b830 added. os.fwalk also runs out of fds at about 500 levels. Avoid GNU-only flags. Because the guard sits inside _remove_run_dir, the finally block can no longer replace the tool result. As hardening, consider a total size/inode quota for the run dir. Add a regression test that creates a tree deeper than PATH_MAX, with a mode-0 directory at the bottom and a symlink to a directory outside the tree, and asserts the run dir is removed and the outside target is unchanged.

title: Unauthenticated code-exec MCP endpoint accepts any Host/Origin (DNS rebinding to a localhost server; unauthenticated 0.0.0.0 exposure in Docker)
description: run_mcp() starts the FastMCP streamable-HTTP transport with no authentication and no Host/Origin validation. In fastmcp 4.0.3 (pinned in uv.lock), settings.http_host_origin_protection defaults to False, so run_http_async does not install HostOriginGuardMiddleware. create_streamable_http_app also always passes TransportSecuritySettings(enable_dns_rebinding_protection=False) to the MCP SDK session manager. The project never overrides either setting and configures no auth provider. The server therefore executes a tools/call run_python_code request that carries an attacker hostname in both Host and Origin, and returns the output. CLI mode binds localhost, and the bind address is the only gate. A web page using DNS rebinding can therefore reach localhost:6400, run code through srt, and read the response. The default srt policy has denyRead []. The executor (current source a80b830) adds only the server working directory to denyRead, so the response can still include any other file the invoking user can read. Docker mode binds 0.0.0.0 (docker-entrypoint.sh), and compose publishes 6400:6400 on all host interfaces. Any network peer can therefore run code without credentials, and so can any web page via rebinding.
root_cause: mcp_server.py:49-56 calls mcp.run_async(transport, stateless, host, port, path, show_banner) without host_origin_protection, allowed_hosts or allowed_origins, and without an auth provider (FastMCP(name=name) at mcp_server.py:17). fastmcp 4.0.3 then falls back to http_host_origin_protection=False (fastmcp/settings.py:280). That skips HostOriginGuardMiddleware (fastmcp/server/http.py:656), and fastmcp explicitly disables the SDK's DNS-rebinding check (http.py:675-680). The endpoint has no Host/Origin guard and no authentication, so the bind address is the only control. DNS rebinding bypasses a localhost bind, and the Docker 0.0.0.0 bind removes that control entirely.
intended_behavior: Only the intended local MCP client, or authenticated clients in a network deployment, can invoke run_python_code. A localhost-bound server rejects requests whose Host/Origin is not loopback or explicitly allowlisted, and a non-loopback bind requires authentication.

trace.description: The CLI binds 'localhost' by default. The HTTP endpoint at <host>:6400/mcp is the lower-trust entry and has no authentication. docker-entrypoint.sh:15 overrides this with --mcp_host=0.0.0.0, and docker-compose.yml:8 publishes 6400:6400.

mcp.run_async(...) is called with no host_origin_protection, allowed_hosts, allowed_origins or auth. fastmcp's default http_host_origin_protection=False applies, so HostOriginGuardMiddleware is not installed, and fastmcp disables the SDK DNS-rebinding check.
run_python_code is registered as a tool with no per-caller authorization.

Caller code runs via subprocess.Popen(srt ...) as the configured user: the invoking user in CLI mode, nonroot in Docker. The per-run srt settings deny reads only of the server working directory on top of the base denyRead []. stdout/stderr and ./output files are returned to the HTTP caller (code_executor.py:254).

evidence.description: run_async call without host/origin protection or auth arguments; FastMCP(name=name) at line 17 has no auth provider
Default bind 'localhost', the only network gate in CLI mode
Docker mode binds 0.0.0.0
Port 6400 published on all host interfaces
denyRead is empty, so sandboxed code can read any file its uid can read
The generated per-run policy adds only the server working directory to denyRead, so other user-readable files stay readable
fastmcp pinned to 4.0.3, whose http_host_origin_protection defaults to False

conditions.description: DNS-rebinding path (CLI/localhost mode): the user running the server visits an attacker-controlled page whose hostname re-resolves to 127.0.0.1, and the browser does not block the request (for example via Private Network Access). This browser step was not exercised locally.

The operator has not set FASTMCP_HTTP_HOST_ORIGIN_PROTECTION or FASTMCP_HTTP_ALLOWED_HOSTS and runs the default http transport. For the direct network path, the server runs in the shipped Docker configuration (0.0.0.0 bind, port published) and the attacker's network can reach it.

execution.attacker_perspective: An unauthenticated HTTP client with no credentials. This is either a web page the local user visits, reaching localhost via DNS rebinding so the request carries the attacker's hostname in Host/Origin, or any network peer of a Docker deployment.

Create a dummy 0644 file /scratch/dummy_v containing VER-DUMMY-8842.
Send the payload to 127.0.0.1:<port> over container loopback with no auth header. Repeat with host='0.0.0.0' (the Docker entrypoint bind).

execution.observed_result: Re-reproduced on current source a80b830 with fastmcp 4.0.3 (installed default http_host_origin_protection=False). Localhost bind, foreign Host/Origin, no auth: HTTP 200, and the result output is 'VER-DUMMY-8842 999', so the code ran as uid 999 through srt plus the new unshare wrapper and returned the dummy file. 0.0.0.0 bind: HTTP 200 with the same output. Control 1 (strict protection, foreign Host): HTTP 421 Misdirected Request. Control 2 (strict protection, Host localhost): HTTP 200 with the same output, so the guard does not break legitimate loopback clients. Control 2 also shows that the Host guard alone does not stop a network peer on a 0.0.0.0 bind, because the peer can send Host: localhost, which is a DEFAULT_HOSTS entry (fastmcp/server/http.py:38). Evidence: agents/ver-httpauth/artifacts/evidence1.txt.

remediation.strategy: Enforce two controls. (1) Always enable FastMCP's Host/Origin guard (host_origin_protection=True), with an operator-supplied allowed_hosts list for deployments reached under a non-loopback name. This closes DNS rebinding against loopback binds. (2) Require bearer-token authentication (FastMCP auth provider), and refuse to start the HTTP transport on a non-loopback bind when no token is configured. The Host guard alone does not protect 0.0.0.0 binds, because it always accepts Host: localhost/127.0.0.1/::1 and any network peer can send those. The Docker image and compose file must then provide MCP_AUTH_TOKEN, and clients send 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'. FullSettings has no allowed_hosts or auth_token fields today, so add both and read them from the environment, which leaves the CLI signature unchanged. In fastmcp 4.0.3, run_http_async accepts host_origin_protection and allowed_hosts, and fastmcp.server.auth.providers.jwt.StaticTokenVerifier exists.

import os


def _env_list(name: str) -> list[str] | None:
    raw = os.environ.get(name, "").strip()
    return [h.strip() for h in raw.split(",") if h.strip()] or None


class FullSettings(CodeSandboxSettings):
    transport: str
    stateless: bool
    port: int
    host: str
    path: str
    log_level: int
    installed_python_dependencies: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    # extra Host values accepted besides loopback (e.g. the Docker service name)
    allowed_hosts: list[str] | None = Field(default_factory=lambda: _env_list("MCP_ALLOWED_HOSTS"))
    # bearer token required from HTTP clients; mandatory for non-loopback binds
    auth_token: str | None = Field(default_factory=lambda: os.environ.get("MCP_AUTH_TOKEN") or None)

from fastmcp.server.auth.providers.jwt import StaticTokenVerifier

_LOOPBACK_HOSTS = {"localhost", "127.0.0.1", "::1"}


async def run_mcp(settings: FullSettings):
    if settings.transport != "stdio" and settings.host not in _LOOPBACK_HOSTS and not settings.auth_token:
        raise SystemExit(
            f"Refusing to serve run_python_code on non-loopback host {settings.host!r} without authentication; set MCP_AUTH_TOKEN."
        )
    auth = (
        StaticTokenVerifier(tokens={settings.auth_token: {"client_id": "mcp-client", "scopes": []}})
        if settings.auth_token
        else None
    )
    mcp = FastMCP(name=name, auth=auth)
    ...
    await mcp.run_async(
        transport=settings.transport,  # ty:ignore[invalid-argument-type]
        stateless=settings.stateless,
        host=settings.host,
        port=settings.port,
        path=settings.path,
        show_banner=False,
        **(
            {"host_origin_protection": True, "allowed_hosts": settings.allowed_hosts}
            if settings.transport != "stdio"
            else {}
        ),
    )
